problemText: Which idea was part of Dalton's original atomic theory of 1803?
choices: Electrons are embedded in a soft sphere of positive charge, like plums in a pudding
Nearly all of an atom's mass is packed into a tiny central nucleus
Atoms are rearranged during a chemical reaction, never created or destroyed
Electrons can hold only certain fixed energies, so they occupy discrete levels
hints: Dalton worked before anyone had detected an electron or a nucleus — his theory is about whole atoms only.
Which statement explains conservation of mass without mentioning any particle inside the atom?

problemText: In a cathode-ray tube the beam bends toward a positively charged plate, and the same negatively charged particle is produced no matter which metal the cathode is made from. What conclusion did Thomson draw from this evidence?
choices: Every atom, of every element, contains the same negatively charged particle, so atoms cannot be indivisible
The positive charge of an atom is concentrated in a tiny central core
Each metal produces its own distinct kind of negative particle
Negative particles exist only in heated metals, not inside ordinary atoms
hints: Two separate clues: the direction of the bend tells you the charge, and 'same particle from every metal' tells you how widespread it is.
If the identical particle comes out of every element tested, it must be a piece of every atom — which contradicts one of Dalton's claims.

problemText: A researcher repeats the alpha-particle scattering experiment using a thin platinum foil and finds that about 1 in 12,000 alpha particles is deflected sharply backward. If Thomson's plum-pudding model had been correct, what should she have observed instead?
choices: About half of the alpha particles would have bounced backward
Every alpha particle would have been absorbed and stopped by the foil
The alpha particles would have been pulled in and captured by the electrons
Essentially every alpha particle would have passed through with at most a tiny deflection, because thinly spread positive charge cannot reverse a fast, heavy particle
hints: In plum pudding the positive charge is smeared through the whole atom and the electrons are far too light to push a heavy alpha particle around.
Ask what force could possibly turn a fast, massive, positive particle around — and whether a thin smear of charge can supply it.

problemText: A sealed tube of neon gas glows when a current passes through it. Sending that light through a prism produces a handful of sharp, separate colored lines instead of a continuous rainbow. Which conclusion does this observation support?
choices: A neon atom contains exactly one electron for each line seen in the spectrum
The electrons in a neon atom can hold only certain energies, so only certain energy drops — and therefore only certain colors — are possible
The nucleus of a neon atom emits the light as it breaks apart
Neon must actually be a mixture of several different elements, each contributing one line
hints: The color of emitted light corresponds to a specific energy. Only a few colors appear, so only a few energies are being released.
Light is released when an electron drops from a higher energy to a lower one. Restricted colors mean restricted energies to drop between.

problemText: Dalton's atomic theory says a chemical reaction only rearranges atoms, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants. In a sealed flask, 4.4 g of propane gas burns completely in 16.0 g of oxygen gas, forming carbon dioxide and water as the only products. If 13.2 g of carbon dioxide is produced, what mass of water is produced, in grams?
hints: The flask is sealed and atoms are only rearranged, so start by adding the reactant masses: 4.4 g + 16.0 g.
That total product mass is split between only two products. Subtract the 13.2 g of carbon dioxide from it.

problemText: Suppose the gold-foil experiment had produced a completely different result: alpha particles emerged spread evenly across every angle, with none passing straight through undeflected. What would that outcome have implied about the structure of the atom?
choices: The atom is mostly empty space with a tiny dense nucleus — the same conclusion Rutherford actually reached
The atom contains no positive charge at all
Positive charge and mass are spread through the atom's entire volume, so there is no empty space for a particle to cross — a pudding-like atom rather than a nuclear one
Electrons must be far more massive than alpha particles
hints: Each observation carries its own conclusion. In the real experiment, which observation was the evidence for empty space — and what does its absence tell you?
If every single particle interacts strongly, then whatever they are hitting must fill the atom rather than sit in a tiny core.

problemText: Two atoms belong to the same element if and only if they contain the same number of which particle?
choices: Neutrons
Protons
Electrons
Protons and neutrons combined
hints: One count is the element's identity — it is the whole-number address printed in each periodic-table box.
Neutrons vary between isotopes and electrons vary between ions, yet the element never changes in either case.

problemText: Iron has atomic number 26. How many protons, neutrons, and electrons are in a neutral atom of iron-56?
choices: 26 protons, 56 neutrons, 26 electrons
26 protons, 30 neutrons, 30 electrons
26 protons, 30 neutrons, 26 electrons
30 protons, 26 neutrons, 30 electrons
hints: The 56 is the MASS number A, not a neutron count. Use neutrons = A − Z.
The atom is described as neutral, so electrons must equal protons.

problemText: Phosphorus has atomic number 15. An atom contains 15 protons, 16 neutrons, and 15 electrons. Which symbol represents this atom?
choices: ³¹₁₅P
³⁰₁₅P
¹⁶₁₅P
¹⁵₃₁P
hints: In full isotope notation the mass number goes on top and the atomic number below.
Mass number = protons + neutrons = 15 + 16, and the atomic number stays 15.

problemText: Atom X has 20 protons, 22 neutrons, and 20 electrons. Particle Y has 20 protons, 20 neutrons, and 18 electrons. Which statement about X and Y is correct?
choices: X and Y are different elements, because their mass numbers are different
X and Y are isotopes of the same element, and Y is also a 2+ ion
X and Y are the same isotope and differ only in charge
Y has been changed into a different element by losing two electrons
hints: Compare the proton counts first — that settles whether they are the same element.
Then handle the two differences separately: neutrons differ (isotopes) and electrons differ from protons in Y (an ion).

problemText: A monatomic ion has a mass number of 139, contains 54 electrons, and carries a charge of 3+. How many neutrons does this ion contain? Type your answer as a number.
hints: A 3+ charge means the atom LOST three electrons, so protons = electrons + 3.
That gives 57 protons. Now use neutrons = mass number − protons.

problemText: A single particle contains 24 protons, 28 neutrons, and 21 electrons. Chromium (Cr) has atomic number 24 and iron (Fe) has atomic number 26. Which symbol represents this particle?
choices: ⁵²Cr³⁻
²⁸Cr³⁺
⁵²Fe³⁺
⁵²Cr³⁺
hints: Work through the three counts one at a time: protons fix the element symbol, protons + neutrons fix the superscript mass number, and protons − electrons fix the charge.
24 protons − 21 electrons leaves a net of 3 more positives than negatives, and the mass number is 24 + 28, not 28.

problemText: The periodic table lists chlorine's atomic mass as 35.5 u, yet every individual chlorine atom has a whole-number mass number. What does that decimal value describe?
choices: The mass of one chlorine atom after the mass of its electrons has been subtracted
The abundance-weighted average mass of chlorine's naturally occurring isotopes
The uncertainty in the best available measurement of a single chlorine atom
The average of the mass of a proton and the mass of a neutron
hints: No single atom weighs 35.5 u — the number describes a population, not one particle.
Chlorine on Earth is a mixture of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. What kind of average accounts for how common each one is?

problemText: Element M has exactly two natural isotopes: M-6 with a mass of 6.0 u and 25.0% abundance, and M-8 with a mass of 8.0 u and 75.0% abundance. What is the average atomic mass of M?
hints: Convert each percent to a decimal fraction (0.250 and 0.750) and check that they add to 1 before multiplying.
Compute 0.250 × 6.0 and 0.750 × 8.0, then add the two contributions. The answer must lean toward the more abundant isotope.

problemText: Element R has exactly two natural isotopes: R-63 with a mass of 63.0 u and R-65 with a mass of 65.0 u. R's average atomic mass is 63.5 u. What does this tell you about R's natural mixture?
choices: R-63 is much more abundant than R-65
R-65 is much more abundant than R-63
The two isotopes are present in nearly equal amounts
There must be a third isotope with a mass below 63.0 u
hints: The weighted average always lands between the two isotope masses, closer to whichever one is more common.
63.5 sits very close to 63.0 and far from 65.0. Which isotope is doing nearly all of the pulling?

problemText: Gallium has exactly two natural isotopes: gallium-69, with a mass of 69.0 u, makes up 60.0% of natural gallium, and gallium-71, with a mass of 71.0 u, makes up the rest. What is gallium's average atomic mass?
hints: Only one abundance is given. The two fractions must add to 1, so find the abundance of gallium-71 first.
Use 0.600 × 69.0 and 0.400 × 71.0, then add. A plain average of 70.0 ignores the abundances entirely.

problemText: Element X has three natural isotopes: X-24 with a mass of 24.0 u and 80.0% abundance, X-25 with a mass of 25.0 u and 10.0% abundance, and X-26 with a mass of 26.0 u and 10.0% abundance. Calculate the average atomic mass of X in u. Type your answer as a number to one decimal place.
hints: The method does not change with three isotopes: multiply each mass by its decimal fraction, then add all three contributions.

problemText: Element Z has exactly two natural isotopes: Z-10 with a mass of 10.0 u and Z-12 with a mass of 12.0 u. The average atomic mass of Z is 11.5 u. What is the percent abundance of Z-10?
hints: Call the fraction of Z-10 x. Then the fraction of Z-12 is 1 − x, and 10.0x + 12.0(1 − x) = 11.5.
Simplify to 12.0 − 2.0x = 11.5, solve for x, then convert the fraction to a percent. Check your answer against the fact that 11.5 sits much nearer 12.0.

problemText: What is the maximum number of electrons that a single p subshell can hold?
hints: Capacity comes from the number of orbitals: a p subshell has 3 orbitals.
The Pauli exclusion principle allows at most 2 electrons per orbital, so multiply.

problemText: Silicon has atomic number 14. Which is the correct ground-state electron configuration of a neutral silicon atom?
choices: 1s² 2s² 2p⁸ 3s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3d²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3p⁴
hints: Every choice sums to 14 electrons, so the arithmetic check will not separate them — check capacities and filling order instead.
A p subshell never exceeds 6 electrons, and 3s must be filled before anything goes into 3p or 3d.

problemText: An atom's ground-state electron configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p². How many valence electrons does this atom have?
hints: Valence electrons are ALL the electrons in the highest occupied shell — here, everything with n = 3.
Add the 3s and the 3p electrons together; the n = 1 and n = 2 electrons are core, not valence.

problemText: Potassium has atomic number 19. Which is the correct ground-state electron configuration of a neutral potassium atom?
choices: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁷
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵ 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹
hints: All four choices contain 19 electrons, so only the filling rules can decide — check capacity first, then order.
The Aufbau order follows energy, not shell number: after 3p is completely full, the next electron goes into 4s, not 3d.

problemText: Nickel has atomic number 28. Place its 28 electrons in Aufbau order (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d), then apply Hund's rule to the final subshell: the d subshell has 5 orbitals, and every orbital receives one electron before any orbital receives a second. How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state nickel atom have? Type your answer as a number.
hints: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² accounts for 20 electrons, and every one of those subshells is completely full — full subshells contain no unpaired electrons. How many electrons are left for 3d?
Spread those 8 electrons over the 5 d orbitals: the first 5 go in singly, then the remaining 3 pair up with three of them. Count the orbitals still holding a lone electron.

problemText: An atom has the ground-state electron configuration [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p³, where [Ar] stands for a filled argon core of 18 electrons. Which statement about this atom is correct?
choices: It has 15 valence electrons, because the 4s, 3d, and 4p electrons all lie outside the core
It has 3 valence electrons, because only p electrons count as valence
It has 5 valence electrons — the 4s² and 4p³ electrons in the highest occupied shell — so it tends to gain 3 electrons and form a 3− ion
It has 2 valence electrons, because only the s subshell counts as valence
hints: Valence electrons are the electrons in the highest occupied SHELL number n — so first identify the largest n that appears.
The 3d electrons sit in shell 3, not shell 4, so they are not valence here. Count only the n = 4 electrons, then compare that total with the 8 needed to fill an outer s and p shell.
